findings.source_passage: "I don't know, but I heard that gamboge ghost of a Fedallah saying so, and he seems to know all about ships' charms."
findings.source_locator: Flask's first speech about the ship charm
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'gamboge ghost of a Fedallah' is a highly distinctive, colorful epithet that establishes Melville's voice and the sailors' attitude toward the Parsee; flattening it to 'Fedallah says so' erases a signature image.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain 'gamboge ghost of a Fedallah' verbatim in Flask's speech about the charm.

findings.source_passage: "Why, do ye see, the old man is hard bent after that White Whale, and the devil there is trying to come round him, and get him to swap away his silver watch, or his soul, or something of that sort, and then he'll surrender Moby Dick."
findings.source_locator: Stubb's speech about Ahab bargaining with Fedallah
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is interpretively crucial—it is the sailors' vernacular articulation of Ahab's Faustian bargain, one of the book's central themes, and its comic-ominous voice is irreplaceable.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Stubb's 'swap away his silver watch, or his soul' speech, at least in substance with key phrasing intact.

findings.source_passage: "The devil, switching his hoofs, up and says, 'I want John.' 'What for?' says the old governor. 'What business is that of yours,' says the devil, getting mad,—'I want to use him.' 'Take him,' says the governor—and by the Lord, Flask, if the devil didn't give John the Asiatic cholera before he got through with him, I'll eat this whale in one mouthful."
findings.source_locator: Stubb's anecdote about the devil visiting the governor
findings.why_it_matters: This extended comedic devil-anecdote is a key voice-establishing digression—Stubb's vernacular theology at its most characteristic—and its complete absence flattens a major tonal set-piece.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the core of Stubb's 'I want John' / Asiatic cholera devil-anecdote; it is too distinctive to reduce to summary.

findings.source_passage: "Do you see that mainmast there?" pointing to the ship; "well, that's the figure one; now take all the hoops in the Pequod's hold, and string along in a row with that mast, for oughts, do you see; well, that wouldn't begin to be Fedallah's age."
findings.why_it_matters: This elaborately comic conceit for Fedallah's infinite age is a signature piece of Melville's vernacular wit and carries interpretive weight about Fedallah's supernatural nature; its absence is a real loss.
findings.suggested_fix: Include at least the mainmast-as-figure-one / hoops conceit for Fedallah's age in the dialogue summary.

findings.source_passage: "Am I the same man that helped kill this whale? Doesn't the devil live for ever; who ever heard that the devil was dead? Did you ever see any parson a wearing mourning for the devil?"
findings.source_locator: Stubb's reply about the devil living forever
findings.why_it_matters: The rhetorical chain of questions is characteristically Melvillean and shows Stubb's comic-theological reasoning; collapsing it loses voice texture.
findings.suggested_fix: Incorporate at least 'who ever heard that the devil was dead?' as a fragment in the dialogue passage.

summary: The draft omits or flattens several key dialogue passages—Stubb's Faustian-bargain speech, the 'gamboge ghost' epithet, the devil-anecdote about John, and Fedallah's-age conceit—losing the sustained vernacular-theological voice that makes this chapter's dialogue central to the book's interpretive architecture.
